title: Dermatoscopy
what: The doctor looks at your moles through a special magnifier with a light, called a dermatoscope. It shows details you cannot see with the naked eye.
why: For a yearly mole check, if you have many moles, if one has changed, bleeds, or itches, or if melanoma runs in your family.
tell_doctor: Which moles have changed, and when
If you or your relatives have had skin cancer
If you have had bad sunburns
If you have had moles removed before

prepare.title: Skin
prepare.text: Do not put on lotion, foundation, or self-tanner before the visit.

prepare.title: Nails
prepare.text: If you have spots on your nails, remove your nail polish.

prepare.title: Check yourself
prepare.text: Beforehand, note or take photos of the moles that worry you.

bring: Past reports and photos of your moles
Lab results, if you have had moles removed
steps: The doctor asks what worries you
You undress down to your underwear so all your skin can be checked
The doctor holds the dermatoscope to each mole that looks unusual
Sometimes the doctor photographs moles to compare later
The doctor tells you what to do: keep watching it, or have it removed
feel: Nothing, just the touch of the device, sometimes with a drop of gel
after: You usually get the results right away
If a mole needs to be removed, you get a referral
Your next check is when the doctor advises, often once a year

faq.q: Which moles should I show the doctor?
faq.a: Ones that grow, change color or shape, bleed, itch, or look very different from the others.
No. It is just a look through a magnifier. No needles, no cuts.
